Understand what the internet really is, how your phone connects to it through mobile data or Wi-Fi, and how to make every data bundle last longer. Then learn to use a browser, search well and read a web address so you can tell a real website from a fake one.

The **internet** is a huge network of computers and devices all over the world, joined together so they can send information to one another. Your smartphone is one of those devices. When you send a WhatsApp voice note, watch a video or check your bank balance, your phone is sending and receiving small pieces of information, called **data**, through this network.

The internet and the Web are not the same thing

People often use the two words for one thing, but they are different. The **internet** is the network itself: the cables, masts, satellites and powerful computers called **servers** that store information. The **World Wide Web** is one service that runs on the internet: the pages you open in a browser, like a news site or a school portal. The Web was invented by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989. WhatsApp, email and online banking apps also use the internet, but they are not web pages.

How your message travels

When you send a photo to your sister in another state, the photo is broken into many small packets. Your phone sends them by radio waves to the nearest **mast** (base station) of your network, such as MTN, Airtel or Glo. From the mast, the packets travel through cables to your network's computers, then across the internet to WhatsApp's servers, and back down to your sister's network and her phone. Her phone puts the packets back together into the photo. All of this usually happens in a second or two.

Much of the internet traffic between Africa and the rest of the world travels through **undersea cables** laid along the ocean floor. Several of these cables land in Lagos, including Google's Equiano cable. This is why a damaged undersea cable can make the internet slow across many countries at once, even when your own phone and network are fine.

No single person or company owns the internet. Each part is owned by someone different: your network owns its masts, cable companies own the cables, and companies like Google or Meta own their servers. A company that sells you access, such as a mobile network or a home broadband provider, is called an **internet service provider (ISP)**. When the internet is down, it is usually one part of this chain, not the whole internet.

Two ways your phone gets online
**Mobile data**: your SIM card connects to your network's masts. You pay for it with a data bundle. It works almost anywhere there is network coverage.

**Wi-Fi**: your phone connects by radio to a nearby router, for example at home, in an office, a church or a hotel. The router itself is connected to the internet. Wi-Fi does not use your data bundle, but someone pays for that connection.

Look at the top of your screen. The bars show how strong your network signal is. Letters next to the bars show the type of mobile connection: **2G or E** is very slow and mostly good for calls and SMS, **3G or H+** is usable for WhatsApp messages, **4G or LTE** is good for video, and **5G** is faster still where it is available. A fan-shaped Wi-Fi symbol means you are connected to Wi-Fi instead.
When pages will not load

First check the icons. No bars or an E means weak coverage: move near a window or outdoors. Then turn Airplane mode on for ten seconds and off again. This makes your phone search again for the strongest mast nearby.
Worked example: reading the icons before a meeting
For example, Halima in Kaduna has a WhatsApp video call with her cooperative at 4pm. At 3:50pm her screen shows one bar and the letter E.
She knows E means a very slow 2G connection, too slow for video.
She walks to the front of the compound, where her screen now shows three bars and 4G.
She turns off Wi-Fi because the neighbour's Wi-Fi she once joined is weak and keeps dropping.
She joins the call and switches her own camera off to keep the call steady.
By reading two small icons and moving 20 metres, Halima turned an impossible video call into a clear one.

Data is measured in **megabytes (MB)** and **gigabytes (GB)**. One GB is about 1,000 MB (networks usually count 1,024 MB as 1 GB). A data bundle gives you a fixed amount of data that must be used before it expires, for example within a day, a week or 30 days. When it runs out or expires, your phone either stops browsing or starts charging your airtime at a higher rate, depending on your network and settings.

Check your balance the safe way

Every network has a short USSD code to check data balance, and an official app (for example the MyMTN or MyAirtel app). Find the correct code on your network's official website or on the back of your SIM pack, and save it in your contacts as "Data balance". Buy bundles only through the official USSD menu, the network's app or your bank app. Never pay a stranger on social media who promises "cheap 50GB for 1,000 naira": this is a common scam.
Five settings that save data

**Android Data Saver**: open Settings, search for "Data Saver" and turn it on. It stops most apps from using data in the background. The exact menu name differs between phone brands, so use the search box at the top of Settings.

**WhatsApp media download**: in WhatsApp go to Settings, then Storage and data, then Media auto-download. Set "When using mobile data" to download nothing, or photos only. You can still tap any video to download it when you choose.
**WhatsApp calls**: in the same Storage and data menu, turn on "Use less data for calls".
**YouTube quality**: while a video plays, tap the settings (gear) icon, then Quality, and choose Data saver or a low number such as 360p.
**Play Store updates**: open Play Store, tap your profile picture, then Settings, Network preferences, and set Auto-update apps to "Over Wi-Fi only".

Auto-renew and "borrowed" data

Some plans renew automatically and take money from your airtime. Some networks also offer data on credit that is repaid from your next recharge. Read the confirmation SMS after every purchase so you know the expiry date and whether it will renew.
Choosing the right bundle

Look at your Data usage screen at the end of a month to see how much you really used. If you used about 3GB, a 30-day plan a little above that is usually cheaper per GB than buying many daily plans. Daily and weekly plans suit people who only go online now and then. Night plans can be cheap, but they only help if you can download things late at night, such as course videos or updates.
Finally, remember that Wi-Fi can save data, but only use trusted Wi-Fi. You will learn in Module 3 why free public Wi-Fi needs extra care, especially for banking.

A **browser** is the app you use to open websites. On most Android phones it is **Google Chrome**. Other browsers include Samsung Internet, Opera Mini and Firefox, and iPhones come with Safari. They all work in a similar way. At the top is the **address bar**, where you can type either a web address (like jamb.gov.ng) or a question you want to search.
A large phone showing a browser window
Chrome and other browsers all share the same basic parts: address bar, tabs and menu.
The parts of a phone browser
**Address bar**: type a web address or search words here.
**Tabs**: each open page is a tab. The square with a number shows how many tabs are open. Tap it to switch or close tabs. Many open tabs slow the phone down.
**Back arrow**: your phone's back button or gesture takes you to the previous page.
**Menu (three dots)**: new tab, history, downloads, bookmarks, settings and Incognito tab.
**Bookmark (star)**: saves a page you will need again, such as your bank's website or your child's school portal.
Incognito is not invisible

An Incognito tab does not save your history on the phone. It does not hide what you do from your network, your employer's Wi-Fi or the websites you visit. Use it on a shared phone, not as a safety tool.
How to search well

A search engine such as **Google** looks through billions of web pages and lists the ones it thinks match your words. The more precise your words, the better the results. Type the important words, not a whole long sentence, and add your location when it matters.

Browsers collect history, saved passwords and small files called **cookies** that remember your logins and settings. On your own phone this is convenient. Reading web addresses, HTTPS and spotting fake websites
Name the parts of a web address and find the real domain
Explain what HTTPS protects and what it does not
Spot common tricks used in fake website addresses
Check a link safely before you open it

Every web page has an address, called a **URL**. Learning to read it is one of the most powerful safety skills on the internet, because fake websites can copy the look of a real bank or company perfectly, but they cannot use the real company's address.
A padlock beside a web server
A secure connection protects data on the way, but only the address tells you who you are talking to.
The parts of a web address
Take this example: **https://www.example.com.ng/account/login**. It has four parts:
**https://** is the method of connection. The s means the connection is encrypted.
**www.** is a subdomain, an optional part at the front.
**example.com.ng** is the **domain**, the name the owner registered. This is the part that tells you who owns the site.
**/account/login** is the path, the page inside that site.

The rule to remember: **read the domain just before the first single slash**. Look at the last part before that slash. In "example.com.ng.secure-login.xyz/" the real domain is secure-login.xyz, not example. Scammers put a famous name at the front so it looks right at a glance.

What HTTPS does and does not do

**HTTPS** encrypts the information travelling between your phone and the website, so people on the same Wi-Fi or network cannot read it. Browsers warn you with "Not secure" when a page uses plain HTTP. In 2023 Chrome replaced the old padlock symbol with a small settings-style icon, because many people believed the padlock meant a site was trustworthy. It never meant that. **A scam website can have HTTPS too.** HTTPS tells you the line is private; it does not tell you who is on the other end.

Treat HTTPS as necessary for logging in, but never as proof that a website is genuine.
Tricks used in fake addresses
**Look-alike spelling**: letters swapped or added, such as "0" for "o", or an extra word like "-verify" or "-ng-update".
**Wrong ending**: the real name with a different ending, such as .net or .xyz instead of the real one.
**Famous name in front**: the brand name at the start, with the real domain hidden at the end.
**Shortened links**: services like bit.ly hide the real address until you open them.
Worked example: checking a link in an SMS
For example, Grace in Port Harcourt receives an SMS: "Your account will be blocked today. Update your BVN at https://gtbank-ng-update.com/verify". She banks with that bank.
She does not tap the link. She presses and holds it to copy it and reads the address instead.
She finds the domain before the first single slash: gtbank-ng-update.com. It is not her bank's official domain.
She opens her bank's official app, which she installed from Play Store, and sees no warning there.
She calls the customer care number printed on the back of her ATM card to report the SMS, then deletes it.
Grace confirmed it was a fake site by reading the domain, and never typed her details anywhere.
Type it or bookmark it
For banking, government portals and anything involving money, do not use links from messages. Type the address you know or use a bookmark you saved yourself, or use the official app.

If you are unsure about a link someone sent on WhatsApp, press and hold it to see the full address. When it is a shortened link, ask the sender what it is, and if the sender is a stranger, simply do not open it.

Prices far below every other seller, for phones, generators or foodstuff.
Payment only by direct transfer to a personal account, with no card payment or pay-on-delivery option.
No physical address, or an address you cannot find on a map, and only a WhatsApp number for contact.
A countdown timer or message saying the offer ends in minutes, to rush you.
A job that asks you to pay a "registration" or "training" fee before you are hired.
When you see two or more of these signs, stop. Search the business name with the word "scam" or "review", ask someone you trust, and remember that a real business will still be there tomorrow.

Email is still how schools, employers, banks, government portals and online courses send official messages. Many services, including WODDI Institute, ask for an email address when you register. **Gmail** is a free email service from Google. One Google account gives you Gmail, the Play Store, Google Drive, Google Photos, YouTube and Google Meet, all with the same email and password.

A busy reader decides in seconds whether to open, answer or ignore your email. Clear emails get faster replies, make a good first impression on employers and customers, and leave a written record you can refer back to. The good news: a professional email follows a simple pattern that anyone can learn.
A person writing a new email
A short, well-structured email is more likely to get a quick reply.
The five parts of a good email
**Subject line**: say what the email is about and what you need. "Request: Certificate copy for Amina Bello, Cohort 3" is better than "Hello" or a blank subject.
**Greeting**: "Dear Mrs Okafor," for someone senior or new to you; "Good morning Tunde," for a colleague you know. If you do not know the name, "Dear Admissions Team,".
**Purpose in the first line**: "I am writing to request a copy of my certificate." Do not make the reader search for your reason.
**Details**: short paragraphs or a short list with dates, reference numbers and what you have attached.
**Closing and name**: a clear next step, then "Kind regards," or "Thank you," and your full name and phone number.

Put the most important information where the reader looks first: the subject and the opening line.
Worked example: rewriting a weak email

For example, Rukayat in Ilorin wants a shop owner to pay for 20 aprons she delivered. Her first draft, with no subject, reads: "hello sir pls I need my money the aprons I brought, you said you will pay."
She adds a subject: "Invoice for 20 aprons delivered 12 May".
She opens with "Dear Mr Adeyemi," and states the purpose: "I am writing about payment for the 20 aprons delivered on 12 May."
She gives the details: "The agreed price was 4,500 naira each, a total of 90,000 naira. The invoice is attached."
She gives a clear next step: "Please make the transfer by Friday 23 May to the account on the invoice, or let me know if you need anything else."
She closes with "Kind regards, Rukayat Bello, Rukayat Aprons, 0803 000 0000 (example number)".
The new email is polite, specific and easy to act on, and gives Rukayat a dated written record of what was agreed.

Try to answer work and customer emails within one working day. If you need more time, send a short reply: "Thank you, I have received this and will respond by Thursday." This keeps trust while you prepare a full answer.

Email can be forwarded and kept forever. Do not write anything in anger, and never put your BVN, card details, PIN or passwords in an email.

**Spam** is unwanted bulk mail, mostly adverts. It is annoying but usually harmless. **Phishing** is different: a message that pretends to come from someone you trust, such as your bank, a delivery company, a network provider or even Google, to trick you into giving away a password, an OTP, card details or money. When it arrives by SMS it is often called **smishing**, and by phone call **vishing**.
A masked figure taking information from a screen
Phishing tries to make you hand over your details yourself, so your judgement is the main defence.
The warning signs
**Urgency or fear**: "Your account will be blocked in 24 hours", "Your BVN has been suspended".
**A prize or money you did not expect**: lottery wins, grants, "you have been selected" for a loan or job.
**A request for secrets**: PIN, OTP, password, card number or BVN. Real banks do not ask for these by email, SMS or call.
**A link or attachment you were not expecting**, especially files ending in .apk, .exe or .zip.
**A sender address that does not match** the organisation, or a free Gmail or Yahoo address claiming to be a bank.
**A generic greeting** like "Dear Customer" and spelling or grammar mistakes.
Check who really sent it

In Gmail, the bold name you see is only a **display name**, and anyone can type any name. Tap the sender's name or the small arrow under it to see the real address. "Zenith Bank Security" sending from zenith-alerts-verify@gmail.com is a scam. Then apply what you learned in Module 1: check the domain in any link by pressing and holding it, without opening it.

Slowing down and checking through a channel you already trust defeats most phishing.
Worked example: a fake delivery SMS
For example, Esther in Abuja is expecting a parcel. She receives an SMS: "Your package is held at our warehouse. Pay 1,250 naira customs fee here to release it" with a link.
She pauses, because the message does not name the shop or the tracking number she was given.
She presses and holds the link and sees a strange domain unrelated to the courier.
She opens the order confirmation email from the shop she bought from and uses the tracking link there instead.
The tracking page shows the parcel is out for delivery with no fee due.
She deletes the SMS and tells her mother, who orders online often, about the trick.
Esther saved 1,250 naira and, more importantly, did not type her card details into a fake payment page.

Tap the three dots at the top right. Choose Report spam. On the web version you can also choose Report phishing.
If you see a yellow or red warning banner from Gmail at the top of an email, trust it.
If a real contact's account sends you a strange link, call them on the phone to warn them their account may be hacked.
If you already clicked or typed

Act at once. If you entered a password, change it from the official app or website and turn on two-step verification. If you shared bank details, a card number or an OTP, call your bank's official number from the back of your card immediately and ask them to block the card or account. Speed matters more than embarrassment.
Phone calls too

A caller who says they are from your bank and asks you to "confirm" an OTP that just arrived is a fraudster, even if they already know your name and part of your account number. Hang up and call the number on your card.

Scammers also reach people through WhatsApp and Facebook, pretending to be friends whose accounts they have taken over, asking for urgent transfers. The same routine works everywhere: pause, verify through another channel such as a phone call, and never send money or codes because of a message alone.

Protecting your accounts, connection and privacy

Lock your accounts with strong passwords, a password manager and passkeys, then add two-step verification so a stolen password is not enough. Learn to use Wi-Fi safely and to set the privacy controls on your phone, Google account, WhatsApp and Facebook.
Strong passwords, password managers and passkeys
Create a long passphrase that is strong and easy to remember
Explain why reusing one password across accounts is dangerous
Save and check passwords with Google Password Manager
Set up a passkey for your Google account

Your password is the main lock on your email, WhatsApp backups, social media and sometimes your money. Criminals do not usually guess passwords one by one. They use computer programs that try millions of common passwords, and lists of passwords leaked from websites that were hacked. A good password beats both.
A large padlock beside a password field
Length and uniqueness, not clever symbols, are what make a password strong.
What makes a password weak
**Personal details**: your name, child's name, birthday, phone number or year, such as Chioma1990. These are easy to find on social media.
**Common patterns**: 123456, password, qwerty, 112233 or your name followed by 123.
**Short length**: anything under 12 characters can be cracked much faster.
**Reuse**: the same password on many sites. If one small website leaks it, criminals try it on your Gmail, Facebook and bank.
The passphrase method

Pick **four random words** that do not belong together, then join them with a number or symbol. For example: **Mango-Bicycle-Rain-Okra7**. It is long, easy to picture and hard for programs to guess. Do not use a famous saying or song line, because those are in criminals' word lists. Use a different passphrase for each important account.

A long, unique passphrase protects you even if another website is hacked.
Let a password manager remember for you

Nobody can remember twenty different strong passwords. A **password manager** stores them securely and fills them in for you. Android phones and Chrome include **Google Password Manager**, linked to your Google account. When you create an account in Chrome, it can suggest a strong random password and save it. You can view saved passwords at **passwords.google.com** after confirming it is you.

Google Password Manager also has a **Password Checkup** that warns you if any saved password has appeared in a known data leak, is weak, or is reused. Run it and change any password it flags, starting with email and banking. This works only if your Google account itself is very well protected, which is why the next lesson on two-step verification matters.
Passkeys: signing in without a password

A **passkey** lets you sign in with the same fingerprint, face scan or screen lock PIN you use to unlock your phone. Your phone keeps a secret key that never leaves the device and only works on the real website or app it was made for. That means a fake website cannot trick you into handing it over, which makes passkeys strong protection against phishing. Google, WhatsApp and many other services now support them.
Make sure your phone has a screen lock (PIN, pattern, fingerprint or face).
Open myaccount.google.com and tap Security.
Find Passkeys and security keys under How you sign in to Google, and tap Create a passkey.
Confirm with your fingerprint or screen lock. Next time you sign in on a new device, Google can ask your phone to confirm instead of asking for a password.
Worked example: fixing reused passwords

For example, Yetunde in Lagos used the password Yetty1988 for Gmail, Facebook, Jumia and a recipe website. The recipe website was hacked, and she later got a Gmail alert about a sign-in attempt from another country.
She changes her Gmail password first to a new passphrase: Kettle-Lagoon-Pepper-Drum4.
She opens passwords.google.com and runs Password Checkup, which shows the old password reused on four sites and found in a leak.
She changes Facebook and Jumia next, using Chrome's suggested strong passwords and saving them in the manager.
She creates a passkey for her Google account so she can sign in with her fingerprint.
Each account now has its own password, and the leaked one no longer opens anything.
Never share it
No genuine bank, network, employer or WODDI staff member will ask for your password or a sign-in code. If someone asks, it is a scam, however official they sound.

You can check whether your email address has appeared in a known data breach at **haveibeenpwned.com**, a free service run by a respected security researcher. If it has, change the password for that site and anywhere you reused it.
If you prefer paper

Writing passwords in a notebook kept safely at home is far better than reusing one weak password everywhere. Keep the notebook out of your handbag and away from visitors, never photograph it, and do not label it "passwords". Your phone's screen lock PIN is also a password: use at least six digits and never your birth year.

WhatsApp accounts are often stolen when someone tricks you into reading out the 6-digit SMS code WhatsApp sends when an account is registered on a new phone. A **two-step verification PIN** blocks this: even with that SMS code, the thief also needs your PIN.
In WhatsApp, open Settings, then Account, then Two-step verification.

WhatsApp will ask for the PIN from time to time to help you remember it.
The "wrong code" trick

A message from a friend's number says: "I sent you a code by mistake, please send it back to me." That code is your own WhatsApp registration code, and sending it hands over your account. Never share any code that arrives on your phone.
Facebook, Instagram and banks

On Facebook and Instagram, open Accounts Center, then Password and security, then Two-factor authentication, and choose an authentication app or SMS. Nigerian bank apps use their own second steps, such as a transaction PIN, a one-time code by SMS or email, a hardware token, or a code generator inside the app. Set these up through your bank's official app or branch, and never share the codes.
Worked example: a stolen password that failed
For example, Patience in Benin City typed her Gmail password into a fake login page by mistake. She had turned on 2-Step Verification with Google prompts a month earlier.
Minutes later her phone shows: "Is it you trying to sign in? Device: Windows, location: another country."
She taps No, it's not me. Google blocks the sign-in.
Google guides her to change her password, and she uses a new passphrase.
She opens Security Checkup and signs out of any devices she does not recognise.
The thief had her correct password but could not get in, because the second step was on Patience's phone.
Changing phones

Before you sell, give away or reset a phone, make sure your authenticator codes and Google prompts are moved to the new phone, and keep your backup codes handy. Google Authenticator can sync codes to your Google account so they are not lost with the phone.

Start with your email, because email is used to reset almost every other account. Then do WhatsApp, Facebook and your bank. It takes about ten minutes per account and is one of the most effective things you can do for your safety online.

Two-step verification sometimes feels like an extra hurdle, but you only meet it on new devices or unusual sign-ins. On your own phone, you rarely notice it. If you are helping an older relative, set up Google prompts for them, because tapping Yes or No is easier than typing codes.

If you ever get a sign-in prompt or code that you did not ask for, it means someone has your password. Tap No or ignore the code, then change your password straight away. Do not approve a prompt just to make it go away.

Using Wi-Fi and hotspots safely
Explain the risks of free public Wi-Fi
Decide which tasks are safe on public Wi-Fi and which are not
Secure a home router, MiFi or phone hotspot with a strong password

Wi-Fi saves your data bundle, which makes free Wi-Fi at hotels, eateries, airports, malls and event venues very attractive. The risk is that you do not control the network. Anyone can create a Wi-Fi network and give it a trusted-sounding name such as "Hotel Guest Free" or "Airport WiFi". Whoever runs the network can see which websites you visit and may try to show you fake login pages.
A woman using her phone while travelling
Public Wi-Fi is handy on the go, but it belongs to someone else.
What public Wi-Fi exposes
**Fake networks**: a criminal sets up a network with the same name as the real one, so your phone joins the wrong one.
**Snooping**: on websites without HTTPS, people on the same network can read what you send.
**Fake login pages**: a "sign in to use Wi-Fi" page that asks for your Google or Facebook password.
**Shared networks**: other devices on the same Wi-Fi can try to connect to your phone if sharing features are left on.

HTTPS, which you met in Module 1, now protects most websites and apps, so public Wi-Fi is much safer than it used to be. Still, a fake network can trick you, and you cannot always tell. The safe habit is simple: **use public Wi-Fi for low-risk things, and switch to mobile data for anything involving money or passwords**.

Reading news: fine
Watching course videos: fine
Logging into email: use data
Banking and payments: use data
Need to type passwords or pay
Everyday use
The more a task involves passwords or money, the more you should switch from public Wi-Fi to mobile data.
Safe habits on public Wi-Fi
Ask staff for the exact network name and password, and check it matches before you join.
Never type your email, bank or social media password into a Wi-Fi sign-in page. A genuine venue page asks only for a code, phone number or room number.
Do banking, transfers and shopping on mobile data, not public Wi-Fi.
If Chrome shows "Not secure" or a certificate warning, close the page.
When you leave, go to Settings, Wi-Fi, tap the network and choose Forget, so your phone does not reconnect automatically.
Stop automatic joining
In your Wi-Fi settings, turn off options like "Connect to public networks" or "Auto reconnect" for networks you do not own. Your phone will then only join networks you choose each time.
Securing your own Wi-Fi, MiFi or hotspot

Many families and small businesses share internet through a home router, a portable MiFi device or a phone's **personal hotspot**. If it has a weak or no password, neighbours can use your data and may see your devices. Protect it like this:
Set the security type to **WPA2** or **WPA3** (never "Open" or the old WEP).
Use a long Wi-Fi password, for example a four-word passphrase.
Change the default admin password printed on the router or MiFi sticker. The admin page address is usually printed on the sticker too.
Change the network name to something that does not include your name, house number or business.

Many Nigerian women now receive and send money through bank apps, USSD codes and fintech apps such as OPay, Moniepoint and PalmPay. These tools are convenient and generally safe when used carefully. Most money lost online is not lost because criminals broke the bank's systems, but because they tricked someone into sharing a code or took control of their phone number.

How a SIM-swap scam works

Your bank sends one-time passwords (**OTPs**) and alerts to your phone number. In a **SIM swap**, a criminal convinces or bribes someone at a network outlet to move your number onto a new SIM card in their possession, often using details they gathered from phishing or social media. Your own SIM stops working. Now the criminal receives your OTPs and can reset passwords or approve transfers.

The attack is fastest in the first hours after your SIM goes dead, so speed is your defence.
Warning signs
Your phone suddenly shows **No service** or **SIM not registered** for a long time while people around you on the same network have signal.
You get an SMS saying your SIM replacement request has been processed when you made none.
You stop receiving calls and SMS, while friends say your phone rings or goes to voicemail.
You get bank emails about sign-ins or transfers you did not make.
Emergency plan: act within minutes
Borrow another phone and call your network's customer care to report a possible SIM swap and ask them to block the number.

Call your bank's official number (from the back of your card or saved in advance) and ask them to freeze your account and cards. Many Nigerian banks have a short emergency USSD code to block your account; find yours on the bank's official website today and save it.
Change your email password and check your email's 2-Step Verification, because email is used to reset bank logins.
Visit your network's office with your ID to recover your number, and your bank to report the fraud in writing.
Keep a record of times, calls and reference numbers for any complaint.

Today, save your bank's fraud line and emergency block code in your phone contacts and also write them on paper at home. During a SIM swap your phone may not work, and you will need the numbers to call from another phone.

Your PIN, OTP, password and BVN should never be told to anyone, including callers who say they are bank staff, network staff, or officials. Banks repeatedly warn customers that they will never ask for these. Anyone who asks is a fraudster.

Where your bank or email allows it, use an authenticator app, Google prompts or a passkey instead of SMS codes for signing in, as you learned in Module 3. This means a stolen phone number alone is not enough to break in. Also avoid posting your phone number together with your full name, date of birth and bank name online, since these details help criminals impersonate you at a network outlet.

Another costly mistake is sending money to the wrong account number. Always read the account name your app shows before you confirm. If money goes to the wrong person, contact your bank at once with the transaction details and ask them to start a recall; it is not guaranteed, but early reports have the best chance.
